antipsychotics.name: Antipsychotics
antipsychotics.scope: First-generation vs second-generation, extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, QTc prolongation
antipsychotics.core: Dopamine-modulating drugs treat psychosis and mania; selection depends on motor, metabolic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and hematologic risks.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Psychosis, mania, agitation; **SGA first-line**; **clozapine** if resistant or recurrent suicidality
FGA: mainly D2 antagonism; SGA: D2/5-HT2 effects, varying by agent
Quetiapine sedation → switch to aripiprazole; obesity → ziprasidone, not olanzapine/clozapine

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Nigrostriatal blockade → movement disorders; tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin elevation
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist; haloperidol high-potency FGA, chlorpromazine low-potency FGA
Chronic D2 blockade → receptor supersensitivity → tardive dyskinesia; can worsen after stopping

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Fever, **lead-pipe rigidity**, autonomic instability, high CK → NMS; stop drug, supportive ICU care
Severe NMS: dantrolene/bromocriptine; olanzapine/clozapine: weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia
Risperidone: ↑prolactin; ziprasidone: ↑QT; clozapine: neutropenia, myocarditis, ileus, seizures

rows.label: Avoid
items: Lewy body/Parkinson disease: severe sensitivity; specialist-selected quetiapine/clozapine if essential
Dementia: ↑mortality, falls; dangerous behavior after safer measures → low-dose **quetiapine**/risperidone, not benzodiazepines

rows.label: Interactions
items: Other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte depletion → torsades; sedatives/alcohol increase CNS depression
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine block dopamine: same EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS; avoid after NMS

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Weight/BMI, BP, glucose/A1c, lipids; movement examinations; **ANC with clozapine**
ECG for cardiac/QT risks; prolactin when symptomatic; ask about bowel function
Clozapine + ANC <1000 → **hold clozapine**, not dose reduction; ANC 1000–1499 → continue, closer monitoring

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia**; valbenazine/deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors
Akathisia can mimic worsening agitation; increasing antipsychotic dose can worsen it
Low-potency FGAs: more orthostasis/anticholinergic effects; high-potency FGAs: more EPS

table.title: Extrapyramidal syndromes
rows: Stop/switch culprit first; benztropine or amantadine

antipsychotics.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [FDA clozapine monitoring update](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-removes-risk-evaluation-and-mitigation-strategy-rems-program-antipsychotic-drug-clozapine); other effects established teaching.

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.scope: Rate and rhythm control, stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc), unstable AF, embolic complications
atrial-fibrillation.core: Disorganized atrial activation produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm and left atrial appendage thromboembolism risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, hypertension, heart failure, coronary disease, obesity, sleep apnea
Hyperthyroidism, alcohol binges, infection, postoperative stress, mitral valve disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Palpitations, exercise intolerance, dyspnea; sometimes incidental or first detected after stroke
★ **Hypotension, ischemic chest pain, pulmonary edema, altered mentation** → unstable AF
Very rapid irregular wide-complex rhythm suggests preexcitation; ordinary AV nodal blockers can be dangerous

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pulmonary-vein ectopic triggers plus atrial remodeling sustain reentry
Loss of atrial contraction reduces filling; persistent tachycardia can impair LV function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG: absent discrete P waves**, variable RR intervals; document rhythm rather than pulse alone
TSH, electrolytes, renal function; transthoracic echocardiogram for ventricular function and structural disease
Intermittent symptoms → ambulatory rhythm monitoring; assess reversible triggers

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → **synchronized cardioversion**; do not delay for anticoagulation or TEE
Stable rate control: metoprolol or diltiazem; avoid diltiazem/verapamil with reduced EF
Decompensated HF: digoxin or amiodarone; preexcited AF: procainamide or cardioversion, no AV nodal blockers
Rhythm control for symptoms, early disease, or HF: cardioversion, selected antiarrhythmics, catheter ablation
★ Duration ≥48 hours/unknown: **3 weeks anticoagulation or TEE** before elective cardioversion; ≥4 weeks afterward

rows.label: Complications
items: **Top risk factor for cardioembolic stroke**, above age/hypertension; limb/gut emboli; tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
Anticoagulant bleeding; rhythm drugs may cause proarrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Long-term anticoagulation: **CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 men/≥3 women**; consider one point lower
Apixaban/other DOAC preferred; mechanical valve or moderate/severe rheumatic mitral stenosis → warfarin
Weight reduction, BP/OSA treatment, limit alcohol
Aspirin no substitute for anticoagulation; adding aspirin to warfarin/DOAC → **more bleeding**, no added stroke protection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atrial flutter: sawtooth atrial activity, often regular 2:1 conduction
Multifocal atrial tachycardia: ≥3 P-wave morphologies, isoelectric intervals

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal → personality change; posterior fossa → ataxia; temporal (Meyer loop) → contralateral **superior quadrantanopia**
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus
★ **Anosmia**, normal nasal exam, frontal release signs, papilledema → **subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion
Astrocytoma grade, prognosis → **degree of histologic anaplasia**, not metastasis; extracranial spread rare

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Tinnitus, imbalance, facial weakness/numbness, altered taste (CN VII, V) → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children
Craniopharyngioma resection disrupts pituitary stalk → **lifelong pituitary hormone replacement**; watch central DI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution; chronic subdural: prior head trauma
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss

table.title: Tumor distinctions
rows: Months of headache, deficits; necrotic, crosses corpus callosum
Woman; extra-axial, uniform enhancement, dural tail; parasagittal
Child; midline cerebellar mass; CSF drop metastases
CPA; insidious, high-frequency unilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Child; ataxia, nystagmus, head tilt, cranial neuropathies

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

cervical-radiculopathy.name: Cervical radiculopathy
cervical-radiculopathy.scope: C5-C8 radiculopathy, cervical disc herniation, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, LMN arm and UMN leg signs, Spurling test, conservative management, MRI cervical spine, surgical decompression
cervical-radiculopathy.core: Neck pain radiating down one arm with a dermatomal sensory deficit and reduced corresponding reflex.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Disc herniation in younger adults; osteophytes and foraminal narrowing with aging
Repetitive neck loading, smoking, prior cervical injury

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Spurling test**: extension, ipsilateral rotation, axial compression reproduce arm symptoms
Shoulder abduction may relieve root pain
★ **Myelopathy**: hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, LMN arms plus UMN legs; late bladder dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Root compression → segmental weakness; central canal stenosis → spinal cord dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: Map strength, sensation, reflexes; examine gait, plantar responses, Hoffmann sign
★ **Cervical MRI**: myelopathy, progressive deficit, cancer/infection concern, or failed conservative care
EMG/nerve conduction studies if localization uncertain; sensory responses usually preserved in radiculopathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **NSAIDs + physical therapy**, activity modification; most improve within weeks
Persistent disabling root pain → consider epidural steroid injection or surgical referral
Cord compression or progressive motor deficit → urgent spine evaluation for decompression
Avoid cervical manipulation with suspected myelopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent denervation and muscle atrophy; untreated cord compression → irreversible disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: Ergonomic adjustments, neck strengthening, smoking cessation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Carpal tunnel: median hand symptoms, positive Phalen, no neck provocation
Rotator cuff disease: painful shoulder motion, preserved distal neurologic examination
Brachial plexopathy: multiple roots/nerves, abnormal sensory nerve responses
ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs, no sensory loss

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age: strongest Alzheimer risk; early-onset first-degree family history; Down syndrome (APP triplication)
Vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Alzheimer: hippocampal loss → poor delayed/episodic recall; **nucleus basalis of Meynert** loss → acetylcholine deficit
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval, preserved independence → reassurance; MCI: objective deficit, independence preserved
Typical Alzheimer: clinical diagnosis after routine labs/imaging; **APOE genotyping not indicated**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy/Parkinson disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA
Parkinson dementia psychosis/agitation → **quetiapine** over haloperidol; clozapine needs agranulocytosis monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage
Parkinson disease: dementia strongest predictor of nursing home placement and mortality

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Visuospatial deficit, e.g., failed pentagon copy → **no car keys** until formal driving assessment
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

diabetic-neuropathy.name: Diabetic neuropathy
diabetic-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, foot ulcer prevention, pharmacotherapy (duloxetine, pregabalin, TCAs)
diabetic-neuropathy.core: Diabetes damages sensory, motor, and autonomic nerves; identify the pattern, exclude additional causes, relieve pain, and protect insensate feet.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long diabetes duration, chronic hyperglycemia, smoking, kidney disease, dyslipidemia
Alcohol excess and metformin-associated B12 deficiency may coexist and worsen symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Acute asymmetric weakness, marked motor loss**, or rapid progression → investigate another cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Metabolic and microvascular injury damages peripheral axons; longest nerves affected first
Loss of protective sensation plus deformity/ischemia → repetitive unnoticed trauma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **10-g monofilament + vibration/pinprick/temperature**, ankle reflexes; inspect skin, deformity, pulses
Screen at type 2 diagnosis, 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, then at least annually
Check B12, TSH, renal function when evaluating neuropathy; consider serum electrophoresis if unexplained
Atypical pattern → nerve conduction studies; gastroparesis → exclude obstruction, gastric-emptying study
New third-nerve palsy → urgent vascular imaging; pupil sparing cannot reliably exclude aneurysm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain → **duloxetine or pregabalin**; gabapentin or TCAs (nortriptyline, amitriptyline) alternatives
Avoid TCAs with arrhythmia, urinary retention, frailty; avoid opioids for routine chronic neuropathic pain
Improve glycemic management; no drug reliably restores established sensory loss
Orthostasis → hydration, compression, medication review; persistent symptoms → midodrine
Gastroparesis → small low-fat meals, short-term metoclopramide; erectile dysfunction → sildenafil unless nitrates

rows.label: Complications
items: Painless ulcers, osteomyelitis, amputation, Charcot arthropathy
Falls, burns, painless MI; metoclopramide → tardive dyskinesia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection, protective footwear**, podiatry for callus/nail care; never walk barefoot
Regular foot exams, smoking cessation; warm swollen neuropathic foot → off-load and assess Charcot/infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: posterior column findings, elevated methylmalonic acid
Lumbar disc radiculopathy: back pain radiating down leg, root-specific weakness
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses, ischemic skin changes

diabetic-neuropathy.evidence: Not checked online; established diabetes neuropathy screening and management teaching.

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Burning/numb feet, reduced vibration and ankle reflexes
Orthostasis, tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder/sexual dysfunction, hypoglycemia unawareness
Acute isolated nerve deficit; often reversible
Unilateral belt-like burning pain, one truncal dermatome

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.scope: Focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, EEG findings, antiepileptic therapy (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine), lifestyle counseling
epilepsy.core: Recurrent unprovoked seizures reflect epilepsy; classify focal versus generalized onset before choosing a maintenance antiseizure drug.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, developmental lesions, genetic predisposition
Sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal and missed drugs can precipitate seizures; provoked seizures alone ≠ epilepsy

rows.label: Clues
items: Focal onset: aura, unilateral motor activity, automatisms or impaired awareness; may evolve bilaterally
Generalized tonic-clonic: abrupt loss of consciousness, stiffening/jerking, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury
Absence: staring, immediate recovery; JME: morning myoclonus ± generalized convulsions
Infantile spasms: flexion clusters, **hypsarrhythmia** on EEG; standard antiseizure drugs ineffective

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormally synchronized cortical neuronal discharges impair awareness, sensation or motor function
Excitatory/inhibitory imbalance may arise from structural lesions or inherited channel/network dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI** after unprovoked seizure; normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy
Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, or one with high recurrence risk/defined syndrome
Check glucose/electrolytes and provoking causes; urgent CT for trauma, focal deficit or persistent altered consciousness
Absence: generalized **3-Hz spike-wave**, provoked by hyperventilation; JME: generalized polyspike-wave
Child, nocturnal facial twitching/drooling, speech arrest + **centrotemporal spikes** → benign rolandic epilepsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Convulsion **≥5 minutes** → airway/glucose, **lorazepam**, then IV levetiracetam/fosphenytoin/valproate
Focal epilepsy → lamotrigine or levetiracetam; generalized tonic-clonic/JME → broad-spectrum agent
★ Valproate effective for generalized syndromes; **avoid when pregnancy possible** if alternatives effective
Pure absence → ethosuximide; absence + tonic-clonic → broad-spectrum drug; infantile spasms → **ACTH or vigabatrin**
Avoid carbamazepine/phenytoin for absence/myoclonic syndromes; drug-resistant focal disease → surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Status epilepticus, injury, aspiration, SUDEP; valproate → hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity
Lamotrigine → serious rash with rapid titration
Levetiracetam → irritability/mood symptoms; depression history + high recurrence risk → continue, monitor mood
Erythromycin (CYP3A4 inhibitor) ↑carbamazepine → ataxia, somnolence, diplopia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adherence, regular sleep, avoid alcohol excess; no abrupt drug withdrawal
Driving restrictions follow local law; no unsupervised swimming/heights; preconception folate and drug review
Pregnancy lowers antiseizure levels; breakthrough seizures → **increase current drug dose**, avoid switching

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syncope: prodrome, rapid recovery; brief jerks possible
Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG confirms typical event without epileptic correlate

table.title: Focal seizure localization
rows: Epigastric/olfactory aura, lip-smacking automatisms; superior quadrantanopia

epilepsy.evidence: Pregnancy recommendations checked 2026-10-30: [AAN/AES/SMFM 2024](https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/5170); classification established teaching.

giant-cell-arteritis.name: Giant cell arteritis
giant-cell-arteritis.scope: Giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, vision loss
giant-cell-arteritis.core: New headache with jaw claudication or visual symptoms after age 50 requires immediate glucocorticoids to prevent irreversible blindness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, female sex, Northern European ancestry; frequently overlaps polymyalgia rheumatica
Age <50 makes this diagnosis very unlikely

rows.label: Clues
items: Scalp tenderness, abnormal temporal artery, fever, weight loss, fatigue
★ **Transient monocular loss, diplopia, or sudden painless visual loss** → ocular ischemia
PMR: bilateral shoulder/hip aching, morning stiffness >45 minutes; true muscle strength preserved

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Granulomatous inflammation of large/medium arteries → intimal proliferation and ischemic narrowing
Posterior ciliary artery involvement causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ESR/CRP and CBC**: inflammation, thrombocytosis, normocytic anemia support; normal markers do not fully exclude
★ **Temporal artery biopsy** confirms; skip lesions can cause false negative, so obtain adequate segment
Ultrasound halo sign useful in experienced centers; arrange testing promptly after treatment begins
Assess pulses, arm pressures, bruits; CTA/MRA for suspected aortic/branch-vessel involvement
PMR: elevated inflammatory markers, normal CK; screen all PMR patients for cranial/visual symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected cranial GCA → **high-dose oral prednisone now**, before biopsy
★ Threatened or established visual loss → **IV methylprednisolone** urgently; ophthalmology consultation
Taper slowly with symptom/marker monitoring; tocilizumab can reduce steroid exposure in selected patients
Isolated PMR → lower-dose prednisone, no biopsy unless cranial/visual symptoms; no prompt improvement → reconsider diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent blindness, often sequential fellow-eye involvement; stroke, aortic aneurysm/dissection
Prolonged steroids → infection, diabetes, cataracts, osteoporosis; IL-6 blockade can suppress inflammatory markers

rows.label: Prevention
items: Bone protection and fracture-risk assessment during prolonged steroids; monitor BP/glucose
Educate about recurrent visual symptoms, jaw pain, limb claudication; evaluate aorta over time

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy: vascular risks, no systemic inflammatory syndrome
Myositis: objective proximal weakness, elevated CK
TMJ disease: local joint pain/clicking rather than chewing-induced ischemic fatigue

giant-cell-arteritis.evidence: Not checked online; established rheumatologic emergency and PMR management.

guillain-barre-syndrome.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
guillain-barre-syndrome.scope: Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni), albuminocytologic dissociation, IVIG or plasma exchange
guillain-barre-syndrome.core: Rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with reduced reflexes after infection suggests immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy; respiratory and autonomic monitoring are immediate priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Campylobacter gastroenteritis, respiratory viral infection, CMV; typically 1–3 weeks earlier
Rare postvaccination association; infection poses greater risk than routine vaccination

rows.label: Clues
items: Leg weakness ascends over days, paresthesias, back/radicular pain, bilateral facial weakness
★ **Areflexia with flaccid weakness**; sensory complaints usually exceed objective sensory loss
★ **BP swings, arrhythmias, urinary retention**, bulbar dysfunction indicate severe disease
Miller Fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; maximal weakness usually within 4 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Molecular mimicry triggers antibodies against peripheral nerve components
Demyelinating conduction block most common in US; axonal variants also occur

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serial **forced vital capacity and inspiratory force**; pulse oximetry misses early ventilatory weakness
LP: **↑protein with few cells**; CSF may be normal during first week
Nerve conduction studies: slowing/conduction block or axonal loss; normal early studies do not exclude
Marked CSF pleocytosis, sensory level, or early sphincter dysfunction → reconsider mimics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Admit for telemetry, swallowing evaluation, frequent strength and breathing assessments
Declining FVC, often <20 mL/kg, weak cough/bulbar dysfunction → **early elective intubation**
★ **IVIG or plasma exchange** for nonambulatory, rapidly progressive, or significant respiratory/bulbar disease
Do not combine routinely; **glucocorticoids do not help**
DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, nutrition, pain control, PT; avoid succinylcholine because hyperkalemia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, aspiration, lethal dysautonomia, VTE, pressure injuries
Residual weakness, neuropathic pain, prolonged fatigue; recovery usually spans months

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prophylaxis; early rehabilitation and immobilization precautions reduce secondary injury
Monitor for treatment-related fluctuations; progression beyond 8 weeks raises concern for CIDP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Transverse myelitis: sensory level, early bladder dysfunction, eventual hyperreflexia
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness, normal reflexes and sensation
Botulism: descending paralysis, pupillary dysfunction, preserved sensorium

guillain-barre-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established neurology teaching.

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection 2–4 weeks post-exposure: fever, rash, sore throat, **mucosal ulcers**, diarrhea, generalized lymphadenopathy
Weight loss, thrush, recurrent candida/herpes, **extensive adult molluscum** → test HIV; dysphagia → candidal esophagitis
Child/teen: chronic fever/diarrhea, poor growth, generalized nodes, splenomegaly, **polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB, pregnancy testing, **cervical cytology**
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count
Prenatal: opt-out screening; refusal → counsel, re-offer later; never test without consent

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: **pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin**, else TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, ophthalmology
Untreated/viremic mother's newborn → **triple ART** ASAP, ideally within 6 h, ≤6 weeks; suppressed mother → zidovudine alone

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary lesion; biopsy after failed empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment, earlier if serology/imaging/CSF PCR disagree
SCID/CVID: low immunoglobulins; SCID lymphopenia, no nodes; perinatal HIV: PJP, thrush, nodes, normal lymphocytes

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; sputum/BAL silver stain
Ring-enhancing mass lesions, edema/mass effect; positive IgG
Cognitive decline; non-enhancing subcortical demyelination, no mass effect

hypertensive-crises.name: Hypertensive crises
hypertensive-crises.scope: Hypertensive urgency, hypertensive emergency, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside
hypertensive-crises.core: Severe BP elevation becomes an emergency when new target-organ injury accompanies it; the number alone does not determine urgency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antihypertensives, CKD, sympathomimetics; clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy, renovascular disease, catecholamine excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Usually **>180/120 mm Hg** with AKI, ACS, pulmonary edema, stroke, or dissection
Encephalopathy: headache, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance; papilledema or retinal hemorrhages

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoregulatory failure → endothelial injury, microangiopathy, tissue ischemia; cerebral vasogenic edema in PRES

rows.label: Dx
items: Repeat correctly sized cuff reading; examine neurologic status, fundi, pulses, heart and lungs
Creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, ECG; troponin with cardiac symptoms
Neurologic symptoms → head CT; suspected dissection → CTA chest/aorta
MRI posterior vasogenic edema supports PRES after hemorrhage exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most emergencies: ICU, titratable IV **nicardipine, labetalol, or nitroprusside**
★ Reduce MAP ≤25% first hour → approximately 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours; then gradual normalization
★ No acute injury: treat pain/anxiety, restart or adjust oral drugs, arrange close outpatient follow-up
Avoid rapid IV lowering for asymptomatic BP; avoid immediate-release nifedipine
Nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use or renal/hepatic dysfunction; monitor closely

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral hemorrhage, renal failure, MI; overly rapid lowering → cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication access and adherence; home BP monitoring; avoid cocaine and amphetamines

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pain/anxiety elevation: improves after trigger control, no acute injury
Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension thresholds differ; avoid applying generic reduction targets

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage (most common) or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids/vitamin A supplements

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late, compensatory; treat ICP, not BP
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema
IIH: **impaired CSF resorption** at arachnoid granulations; ventricles normal/small, no obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings → **LP**: normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction
Recent shunt revision + fever + neutrophilic CSF → **shunt infection**, not community meningitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway/intubation first**, head elevation, IV **hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation and reflexes generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
Proximal weakness + ↑CK → EMG/nerve conduction (myopathic pattern); MRI guides **muscle biopsy**
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs
Guillain-Barré: ascending distal-predominant weakness, areflexia

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness means retinal embolism from the ipsilateral carotid.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Hypertension: greatest modifiable risk factor**; smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: **Broca** nonfluent, poor repetition, intact comprehension; **Wernicke** fluent paraphasias, poor comprehension, no insight
Crossed: **Weber** ipsilateral CN III, contralateral hemiparesis (midbrain); lateral pons: ipsilateral full-face palsy, deafness
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction, often embolic; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF/cardioembolic → oral anticoagulation, timing by infarct/bleeding risk; noncardioembolic → antiplatelet only
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit
Long-term antiplatelet (aspirin allergy → clopidogrel); undertreated hypertension → **intensify antihypertensives**; high-intensity statin

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

table.title: Vascular localization
rows: Occipital: contralateral homonymous hemianopia; macular sparing
Diplopia, vertigo, dysarthria, ataxia, crossed/bilateral signs, coma
Vertigo; ipsilateral Horner/face/ataxia/palate; contralateral body pain-temperature

lead-poisoning.name: Lead poisoning
lead-poisoning.scope: Occupational exposure, moonshine, pediatric lead toxicity, basophilic stippling, motor neuropathy (wrist drop, foot drop), encephalopathy, dimercaprol, succimer chelation
lead-poisoning.core: Exposure-related abdominal colic, anemia, and neurologic dysfunction; children may have developmental injury despite appearing well.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pre-1978 paint dust, contaminated water/soil, imported remedies or pottery; pica increases exposure
Battery manufacture/recycling, construction, firing ranges, moonshine; occupational dust carried home

rows.label: Clues
items: Children: irritability, constipation, learning/behavior problems; severe cases → seizures, encephalopathy
Adults: **motor-predominant neuropathy** with wrist/foot drop, hypertension, renal dysfunction, saturnine gout
Microcytic or normocytic anemia; basophilic stippling supportive but neither sensitive nor specific

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase → impaired heme synthesis
Calcium mimicry disrupts neuronal signaling; deposition in bone creates long-lived stores

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous blood lead level** confirms elevated capillary screening; do not rely on hair testing
★ Pediatric reference **3.5 µg/dL** triggers exposure intervention; no safe childhood level
CBC, iron studies, renal function; abdominal radiograph for suspected ingested lead objects/paint chips
Developmental assessment; assess siblings and household exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove exposure; involve environmental health/toxicology; correct iron deficiency and support calcium intake
Child **45–69 µg/dL**, no encephalopathy → oral succimer with expert supervision
★ Encephalopathy or ≥70 µg/dL → admit; **dimercaprol followed by calcium disodium EDTA**
Radiopaque lead in bowel → polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation when safe
Adults: neuropathy, colic, high level → **calcium disodium EDTA** or succimer; pediatric thresholds don't apply

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent cognitive deficits despite chelation; CKD, infertility, pregnancy complications
EDTA can injure kidneys; disodium EDTA causes fatal hypocalcemia—use calcium disodium formulation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Certified lead abatement, wet cleaning, occupational protective measures; avoid contaminated products
Medicaid childhood screening at 12 and 24 months; otherwise risk/local screening program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron deficiency: low ferritin; can coexist and increase lead absorption
AIP: marked urinary PBG elevation, no characteristic lead anemia

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, no heavy lifting until pain resolves, heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical therapy if pain persists despite NSAIDs; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise
Vascular claudication: calf pain, bicycling too; standing still relieves; weak pulses alone don't exclude stenosis

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates
Shopping-cart sign; pulses usually preserved; MRI confirms

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adults: **S. pneumoniae** most common; seeded by pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis, CSF leak, asplenia
Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; advanced HIV/transplant/chemotherapy → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: subacute, high opening pressure ± CN VI palsy, CSF antigen; TB studies if lymphocytic, low glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal contacts within 7 days of onset → **rifampin or ceftriaxone**; droplet isolation until 24 hours treated
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

mononeuropathies.name: Mononeuropathies
mononeuropathies.scope: Ulnar nerve entrapment (cubital tunnel, Guyon canal, claw hand), radial nerve palsy (wrist drop, Saturday night palsy), peroneal/fibular nerve injury (foot drop), electromyography, splinting, surgical decompression
mononeuropathies.core: Weakness and sensory loss following one peripheral nerve suggest focal compression or injury; preserved muscles supplied proximally help localize the lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Compression, fractures, repetitive motion, tight casts, diabetes; intoxicated immobilization → Saturday night radial palsy
Prolonged elbow flexion, cycling/hypothenar pressure, leg crossing, rapid weight loss
Lithotomy/hip hyperflexion → **femoral** under inguinal ligament; stirrup at fibular head → foot drop
Antecubital hematoma after venipuncture → **median at elbow**; hook of hamate fracture → ulnar in Guyon canal

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Ulnar: **Froment sign**, advanced fourth/fifth-digit clawing; impaired grip and fine finger tasks
Rapid progression, severe pain, multiple noncontiguous nerves → consider vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex
Supraspinatus/infraspinatus atrophy, sensation intact, overhead athlete → **suprascapular** entrapment
Medial plantar laceration → medial toe hyperextension; superficial radial → dorsal web numbness, no wrist drop

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal compression first causes conduction block/demyelination; severe or sustained pressure causes axonal loss
Axonal regeneration is slow; duration and severity predict recovery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Map strength, reflexes, and sensation; compare muscles sharing a root but supplied by different nerves
Persistent/uncertain deficit → **EMG/nerve conduction studies**; denervation may take weeks to appear
Trauma → radiographs; suspected mass/structural entrapment → ultrasound or MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove compression; activity modification, **splinting**, occupational/physical rehabilitation
Ulnar at elbow → night extension splint; radial palsy → wrist-extension splint
Foot drop → ankle-foot orthosis and gait training; inspect cast/brace pressure points
★ Progressive deficit/refractory entrapment → **surgical decompression**; nerve laceration → urgent repair evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Muscle atrophy, fixed contractures, chronic neuropathic pain, falls
Delayed recognition of ongoing compression → irreversible motor deficit

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged elbow pressure, excessive flexion, leg crossing; pad vulnerable areas during surgery/immobility
Optimize diabetes control; ergonomic adjustment and frequent position changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: L5 radiculopathy: root-pattern pain; weakness also in tibialis posterior and gluteus medius
C8 radiculopathy: additional median-innervated muscle weakness, proximal symptoms
Stroke: sudden deficit with upper motor neuron signs or additional central findings

table.title: Localize common lesions
rows: Ulnar hand intrinsics; forearm spared; wrist Tinel
Palmar ulnar digits; dorsal hand spared
Finger extension; wrist extension partly preserved

mononeuropathies.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

mood-stabilizers.name: Mood stabilizers
mood-stabilizers.scope: Lithium (therapeutic range, toxicity, hemodialysis, tremor, nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism), valproate (hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity), carbamazepine, lamotrigine (Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
mood-stabilizers.core: Match the drug to bipolar phase; narrow therapeutic windows, organ toxicity, interactions, and pregnancy risks drive selection.

rows.label: Use
items: Lithium: mania, maintenance, reduced suicide risk; valproate/carbamazepine: acute mania
Lamotrigine: bipolar depression prevention; ineffective for acute mania

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Lithium alters intracellular signaling; anticonvulsants reduce excitatory neurotransmission

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Lithium: **nephrogenic DI**, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism; fine tremor → **propranolol**
Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, weight gain
★ **Lamotrigine rash → stop immediately**; Stevens-Johnson risk increases with rapid titration

rows.label: Avoid
items: Valproate in pregnancy: neural tube defects, impaired neurodevelopment; carbamazepine also teratogenic
Lithium: severe renal impairment, dehydration; pregnancy counseling includes fetal cardiac risk

rows.label: Interactions
items: Thiazides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, NSAIDs increase lithium; volume depletion worsens toxicity
Carbamazepine: CYP induction, reduced contraceptive efficacy; valproate increases lamotrigine levels

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Lithium **12-hour trough**: maintenance usually 0.6–1.0; acute mania 0.8–1.2 mEq/L
Renal function, TSH, calcium; valproate CBC/LFTs; carbamazepine CBC, sodium, LFTs
Carbamazepine: HLA-B*1502 testing with relevant Asian ancestry; agranulocytosis, SIADH, severe rash

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Lithium toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion → stop lithium, IV saline
**Hemodialysis**: seizures/coma, life-threatening arrhythmia, or renal impairment with lithium >4 mEq/L
Consider dialysis: >5 mEq/L, confusion, or clearance >36 hours to <1; monitor rebound

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, **Northern European ancestry**, family history; EBV, smoking, low vitamin D

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular loss, poor color vision, afferent pupillary defect, often normal fundus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired ipsilateral adduction, contralateral abducting nystagmus; convergence intact
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse/optic neuritis → **high-dose IV methylprednisolone**, not low-dose prednisone; refractory → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

narcolepsy.name: Narcolepsy
narcolepsy.scope: Excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, polysomnography and MSLT, hypocretin (orexin) deficiency, modafinil, sodium oxybate
narcolepsy.core: Irresistible sleep attacks despite sufficient nighttime sleep, with emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone strongly suggesting type 1 narcolepsy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually adolescent/young-adult onset; genetic susceptibility with probable autoimmune hypothalamic neuron loss

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Cataplexy**: seconds to minutes of weakness, preserved consciousness; laughter or surprise trigger
Vivid hallucinations at sleep onset or awakening; transient inability to move at sleep transitions
Short naps refreshing; disrupted nighttime sleep; daytime automatic behaviors

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Type 1: deficient hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin → unstable wakefulness and REM intrusion
Type 2: no cataplexy, no demonstrated orexin deficiency

rows.label: Dx
items: Daily sleepiness ≥3 months; sleep diary/actigraphy first to document sufficient sleep
★ Overnight **polysomnography → next-day MSLT**; exclude untreated OSA and sleep deprivation
Mean sleep latency ≤8 minutes plus ≥2 sleep-onset REM periods; preceding PSG can contribute one
Low CSF hypocretin supports type 1; usually unnecessary with characteristic cataplexy and diagnostic testing
Coordinate stimulant/REM-suppressing drug washout before testing; abrupt withdrawal can confound results

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daytime sleepiness → **modafinil**; alternatives methylphenidate, pitolisant, solriamfetol
★ Prominent cataplexy → **sodium oxybate**; venlafaxine can suppress attacks
Oxybate: avoid alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines because of respiratory/CNS depression
Scheduled naps, regular nighttime sleep, workplace/school accommodations

rows.label: Complications
items: Motor vehicle crashes, impaired school/work performance, depression
Modafinil reduces hormonal contraceptive effectiveness; review pregnancy planning

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid driving or hazardous work until sleepiness controlled; reassess driving safety during follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: OSA: snoring, witnessed apneas, abnormal respiratory PSG
Idiopathic hypersomnia: long unrefreshing sleep, fewer sleep-onset REM periods
Syncope/seizure: loss of consciousness or postictal confusion rather than isolated cataplexy

neural-tube-defects.name: Neural tube defects
neural-tube-defects.scope: Anencephaly, spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, Chiari II malformation, maternal serum AFP, amniotic acetylcholinesterase, lemon and banana signs, folic acid prevention
neural-tube-defects.core: Neural tube closure failure by approximately 4 weeks after conception produces cranial or spinal defects; prevention must begin before pregnancy recognition.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low folate, prior affected pregnancy, maternal diabetes/obesity, valproate/carbamazepine, early-pregnancy hyperthermia

rows.label: Clues
items: Midline lumbosacral sac, lower-limb weakness, absent reflexes, bladder dysfunction with neural involvement
★ **Lemon skull and banana cerebellum** on fetal ultrasound suggest open spina bifida/Chiari II
Occult lesions: hair tuft, atypical deep dimple, hemangioma; normal skin does not guarantee normal cord

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Failed neurulation leaves neural tissue unprotected; CSF leakage contributes to hindbrain herniation
Folate supports nucleotide synthesis during rapid embryonic cell division

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Maternal serum **AFP at 15–22 weeks**; elevation → verify dating/number, detailed ultrasound
Open defects elevate AFP; closed occulta may not; cfDNA does not screen neural tube defects
★ Uncertain imaging → amniotic fluid **AFP and acetylcholinesterase**; target anatomy scan at 18–22 weeks
Postnatal spinal ultrasound in young infant or MRI for suspected occult dysraphism/tethered cord

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open spinal lesion: **prone positioning, sterile saline dressing**, avoid pressure/contamination; neonatal neurosurgery
Early closure; assess hydrocephalus, renal function and bladder emptying; intermittent catheterization when neurogenic
Selected prenatal myelomeningocele repair can improve motor outcomes/reduce shunting, with maternal and prematurity risks
Anencephaly → counseling, pregnancy options, and palliative neonatal care; no curative treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Hydrocephalus (Chiari II obstructs CSF), meningitis, orthopedic deformities, neurogenic bowel/bladder, recurrent UTI, kidney injury
Tethered cord may cause progressive weakness or continence changes during growth
Osteopenic insensate legs: new swelling → **X-ray** for occult fracture

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Folic acid 400–800 µg/day** before conception through early pregnancy for average risk
Prior NTD pregnancy → **4 mg/day**, starting ≥1 month before conception through first 3 months
Optimize diabetes, review antiseizure drugs before pregnancy; avoid prolonged overheating

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sacrococcygeal teratoma: solid/cystic mass, not exposed neural placode
Abdominal wall defect: elevated AFP but bowel outside abdomen on ultrasound

table.title: Lesions
rows: Meninges/CSF herniate; cord remains within canal
