neurocutaneous-disorders.name: Neurocutaneous disorders
neurocutaneous-disorders.scope: Neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease, ataxia-telangiectasia
neurocutaneous-disorders.core: Characteristic skin or ocular lesions plus neurologic tumors, seizures, or progressive ataxia suggest an inherited or mosaic multisystem disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, TSC, VHL: autosomal dominant; frequent de novo variants
Ataxia-telangiectasia: autosomal recessive; Sturge-Weber: sporadic somatic mosaicism

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Changing painful neurofibroma**, rapid growth, or new weakness → malignant transformation concern
Early focal seizures or developmental regression → evaluate structural cerebral lesions
NF2: hearing loss/tinnitus; NF1: cutaneous neurofibromas and childhood learning difficulties

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor suppressor dysfunction → hamartomas or neoplasms; ATM defect → impaired DNA repair

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical pattern + genetic testing**; targeted MRI for neurologic or tumor symptoms
NF1: ≥2 criteria; ≥6 café-au-lait macules, size >5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal
TSC: two major features or one major plus two minor; pathogenic variant also diagnostic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic tumors → specialist resection; TSC growing lesions → **everolimus** in selected cases
TSC infantile spasms → vigabatrin; other seizures → antiseizure drugs
Sturge-Weber seizures → levetiracetam; refractory focal epilepsy → surgical evaluation
Ataxia-telangiectasia: rehabilitation, infection treatment; minimize ionizing radiation

rows.label: Complications
items: NF1: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor; VHL: renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
TSC: hydrocephalus, renal hemorrhage; ataxia-telangiectasia: lymphoma/leukemia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**; syndrome-specific eye, hearing, renal, and tumor surveillance
Sturge-Weber: ophthalmology follow-up for glaucoma; NF1: childhood BP and vision monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Isolated café-au-lait macules: no additional diagnostic criteria
Friedreich ataxia: areflexia, cardiomyopathy, no ocular telangiectasias

table.title: Signature findings
rows: Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma
Ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas, cortical tubers, renal angiomyolipomas

neurocutaneous-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical genetics teaching.

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.name: Neuromuscular junction disorders
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.scope: Myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism, repetitive nerve stimulation, autoantibodies
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.core: Fluctuating or descending weakness with preserved sensation localizes to neuromuscular transmission; reflexes, pupils, and exercise response separate major causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: MG: autoimmune disease, thymoma; LEMS: smoking/small-cell lung carcinoma
Botulism: improperly canned foods, injection wounds, infant honey or environmental spores

rows.label: Clues
items: MG: diplopia, ptosis, nasal speech, chewing fatigue; worse late day or repeated activity
LEMS: proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation; transient strength/reflex improvement after exertion
Botulism: cranial palsies → symmetric descending paralysis, autonomic dysfunction; infant constipation and floppy weakness
★ **Bulbar weakness or declining ventilation** → impending respiratory failure even with normal oxygen saturation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: MG: postsynaptic receptor/MuSK autoimmunity; LEMS: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel autoimmunity
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → impaired acetylcholine release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AChR antibodies**, then MuSK if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG
MG → chest CT for thymoma; bedside ice-pack improvement supports ocular disease
LEMS → P/Q calcium-channel antibodies and chest CT for cancer
★ Suspected crisis → serial **forced vital capacity/negative inspiratory force**; not pulse oximetry alone
Botulism → serum/stool/toxin testing via public health; treatment before confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: MG → pyridostigmine, steroid-sparing immunosuppression; thymectomy for thymoma or selected generalized AChR-positive disease
★ Myasthenic crisis → **airway support + IVIG or plasma exchange**, treat precipitant
LEMS → amifampridine and treatment of malignancy; immunotherapy for persistent autoimmune disease
★ Botulism → **heptavalent antitoxin**; infants → human botulism immune globulin; ventilatory support
Wound botulism → debridement/antibiotics; avoid aminoglycosides and magnesium with impaired junctional transmission

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, respiratory arrest; MG immunosuppression → infection; steroids may initially worsen weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review MG-exacerbating drugs; safe food preservation; no honey before age 1 year
LEMS → ongoing cancer surveillance if initial evaluation negative

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: usually ascending weakness and areflexia, possible sensory symptoms
Brainstem stroke: abrupt focal signs; motor neuron disease: fasciculations/UMN signs

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.evidence: Botulism checked 2026-10-30: [CDC clinical guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7002a1.htm); MG/LEMS: established teaching.

parasitic-infections.name: Parasitic infections
parasitic-infections.scope: Strongyloidiasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, cryptosporidiosis, ascariasis, schistosomiasis, pinworm (enterobiasis), cysticercosis, eosinophilia workup, antiparasitic therapy
parasitic-infections.core: Exposure, organ pattern, and immune status identify the parasite; eosinophilia favors tissue-invasive helminths rather than intestinal protozoa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Contaminated food/water, endemic travel, freshwater contact, barefoot soil exposure, household crowding
Steroids/HTLV-1 predispose to Strongyloides hyperinfection; advanced HIV predisposes to persistent cryptosporidiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Ascariasis: transient cough/eosinophilic infiltrates during larval migration; later intestinal or biliary obstruction
Pinworm: nocturnal perianal/vulvar itch, dysuria with normal UA; household clustering
Cysticercosis: seizures or hydrocephalus; ingestion of **T. solium eggs**, not pork cysts
Cutaneous larva migrans: soil contact; pruritic **serpiginous tracks**; animal hookworm larvae → albendazole or ivermectin

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Giardia blunts microvilli → **fat/carbohydrate malabsorption**; invasive protozoa can affect liver, urinary tract, or CNS
Strongyloides autoinfection permits lifelong persistence and dissemination after immunosuppression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unexplained **eosinophilia** → travel/drug history, serial stool O&P, targeted Strongyloides serology
★ Steroids + eosinophilia or infiltrates → **Strongyloides hyperinfection**: **duodenal aspirate** larvae; stool O&P often misses
Diarrhea → stool antigen/PCR for protozoa; single routine O&P can miss infection
★ Pinworm → **morning tape test** before washing; stool testing insensitive
Brain MRI/CT for cysticercosis; eye examination before antiparasitics; assess lesion viability and location

rows.label: Tx
items: Rehydrate; ascariasis → albendazole; bowel obstruction → surgical evaluation before deworming
Pinworm → albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel; repeat after **2 weeks**, treat household simultaneously
★ Viable parenchymal cysticercosis → albendazole ± praziquantel with corticosteroids; seizures → levetiracetam
Calcified brain lesions → no antiparasitic; hydrocephalus → neurosurgical control before cysticidal treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Strongyloides hyperinfection → gram-negative sepsis, respiratory failure; eosinophilia may disappear
Amebic liver abscess; schistosomiasis → portal hypertension or bladder squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen/treat Strongyloides before **immunosuppression** after endemic exposure
Safe water, sanitation, handwashing, footwear; avoid endemic freshwater and untreated swimming water
Neurocysticercosis household contacts → **stool O&P** to find egg-shedding T. solium tapeworm carrier

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea after infection excluded
Drug hypersensitivity: eosinophilia linked to new medication, rash or organ injury

table.title: Exposure → diagnosis and treatment
rows: Camping; greasy stool, bloating; stool antigen
Dysentery, flask-shaped ulcers; stool PCR; abscess → serology
Soil; larva currens, larvae in stool
Ivermectin; hyperinfection requires prolonged daily treatment
Freshwater; hematuria (haematobium), portal fibrosis (mansoni/japonicum); eggs, serology
Confirmed E. histolytica without invasive disease

physiologic-changes-of-aging.name: Physiologic changes of aging
physiologic-changes-of-aging.scope: Neurologic changes, sensory changes (presbyopia, presbycusis), sleep architecture changes (early wake, reduced total sleep), cardiovascular stiffening, renal decline, pulmonary compliance
physiologic-changes-of-aging.core: Normal aging reduces organ reserve; preserved everyday independence distinguishes expected slowing from disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: Gradual changes across systems; marked disability requires evaluation rather than attribution to age
Presbyopia: reduced accommodation; presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ Slower processing and recall; **orientation and learned knowledge preserved**
★ Less slow-wave, more awakenings, earlier timing, less total sleep → **reassure**, no hypnotics
★ Isolated **↓ankle reflexes**, ↓toe vibration, impaired tandem, full strength → normal; no workup

rows.label: Use when
items: Reduced baroreflexes and maximal heart rate → orthostatic susceptibility, reduced exercise capacity
Lower renal clearance → adjust renally eliminated drugs despite normal-looking creatinine
Decreased vital capacity and cough reserve → greater respiratory illness vulnerability

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ **Arterial stiffness** → widened pulse pressure; ventricular relaxation slows
Reduced lung elastic recoil → increased lung compliance; chest wall compliance decreases
Declining concentration/dilution → fluid imbalance; reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Delirium, dementia, falls, incontinence** require evaluation; never inevitable normal aging
Depression or sedatives can explain daytime sleepiness; severe insomnia needs investigation
Unilateral hearing loss, focal weakness, **rotatory nystagmus**, rapid memory loss → disease workup

physiologic-changes-of-aging.evidence: Not checked online; established geriatric physiology.

pituitary-adenomas.name: Pituitary adenomas
pituitary-adenomas.scope: Prolactinoma, acromegaly, nonfunctioning adenoma, pituitary apoplexy
pituitary-adenomas.core: Pituitary tumors cause hormone excess, pituitary failure, or sellar mass effects; determine functional status before choosing medical treatment or surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Most sporadic; MEN1 with associated parathyroid/pancreatic endocrine tumors
Apoplexy may follow tumor hemorrhage/infarction, anticoagulation, pregnancy or major physiologic stress

rows.label: Clues
items: Mass effect → headache and bitemporal hemianopia from optic-chiasm compression
Pituitary failure → fatigue, hypotension, low libido; prolactin-related gonadal suppression may cause infertility
★ **Sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, hypotension** → pituitary apoplexy
GH excess may cause macroglossia, prognathism, enlarged hands/feet and worsening ring/shoe size

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autonomous secretion causes hormone excess; stalk compression interrupts dopamine inhibition, modestly raising prolactin
Expanding sellar tissue compresses normal pituitary and optic pathways; acute infarction can eliminate ACTH reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hormonal assessment → **contrast pituitary MRI**; formal visual fields if lesion abuts chiasm
Check prolactin, IGF-1, AM cortisol, free T4/TSH and gonadal axis; screen cortisol excess when clinically suspected
Elevated prolactin → exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure and dopamine-blocking drugs
Large mass with unexpectedly modest prolactin → dilute assay for **hook effect**
Acromegaly: elevated age-adjusted IGF-1 → failure of GH suppression after oral glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected apoplexy → **IV hydrocortisone immediately**, fluids, urgent MRI and neurosurgical/endocrine assessment
Persistent severe visual deficits or reduced consciousness → urgent decompression after stabilization
★ Replace glucocorticoids **before levothyroxine** when both axes deficient
Prolactinoma → **cabergoline**, even with visual deficits; older exam questions may expect bromocriptine
Residual GH excess after surgery → octreotide/lanreotide or pegvisomant; radiation for selected refractory tumors

rows.label: Complications
items: Visual loss, adrenal crisis, hypogonadism; surgery → CSF leak, diabetes insipidus or panhypopituitarism
Acromegaly → cardiomyopathy, diabetes, sleep apnea, colon neoplasia; cabergoline → nausea/orthostasis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Craniopharyngioma: suprasellar cystic/calcified lesion, often childhood onset
Primary hypothyroidism: ↑TSH/↓free T4 with secondary prolactin elevation; medication effect: no autonomous tumor secretion

pituitary-adenomas.evidence: Prolactinoma checked 2026-10-30: [Pituitary Society consensus, 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-023-00886-5); other sellar emergencies: established teaching.

table.title: Subtype-directed management
rows: Observe if small; surgery for compression

primary-headaches.name: Primary headaches
primary-headaches.scope: Migraine, tension-type, cluster, medication-overuse headache, red flags
primary-headaches.core: Recurrent stereotyped headaches with normal neurologic examination favor a primary syndrome; a new dangerous pattern requires secondary-cause evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, sleep disruption, stress, hormonal fluctuation; alcohol triggers cluster bouts
Frequent rescue analgesic use promotes chronic daily headache

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Thunderclap, fever, papilledema, focal deficit, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum** → evaluate secondary cause
New headache after age 50, positional/Valsalva provocation, progressive change also concerning
Medication overuse: headache ≥15 days/month with sustained frequent acute-drug exposure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Migraine: trigeminovascular/CGRP signaling; aura: cortical spreading depolarization, visual → contralateral occipital lobe
Cluster: hypothalamic/autonomic activation; overuse sustains sensitization and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical stable primary pattern + normal exam → **no routine neuroimaging**
Thunderclap → head CT; negative with persistent SAH concern → LP or CTA
MRI for concerning nonemergent progressive patterns; fundoscopy and full neurologic examination
Overuse >3 months: triptans/opioids/combinations ≥10 days/month; acetaminophen/NSAIDs ≥15 days/month

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe migraine → **sumatriptan + naproxen**, metoclopramide for nausea; avoid triptans with ischemic vascular disease
Frequent migraine → propranolol, topiramate, CGRP drugs; pregnancy → **acetaminophen**; no ergots, topiramate, valproate
★ Cluster attack → **100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan**; prevention with verapamil, ECG monitoring
Tension headache → acetaminophen/NSAID; recurrent chronic disease → amitriptyline, behavioral treatment
Medication overuse → withdraw culprit, start prevention; taper opioids/barbiturates rather than abrupt withdrawal

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic migraine, functional disability, status migrainosus; analgesic toxicity
Estrogen-containing contraception increases stroke concern in migraine with aura
Triptan + **ergotamine within 24 hours** → additive vasoconstriction: prolonged vasospasm, MI, stroke

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Regular sleep/meals, exercise, headache diary**, limit rescue-drug days
Avoid opioids for routine primary headache; identify personal rather than universal dietary triggers
Migraine escalation after starting estrogen, normal exam → **stop estrogen** before imaging or added analgesics

rows.label: Mimics
items: GCA: age >50, jaw claudication/visual symptoms
Acute glaucoma: red painful eye, halos, high pressure; sinusitis: purulence and objective sinus findings

primary-headaches.evidence: Not checked online; established headache classification and generalist management.

prion-disease.name: Prion disease
prion-disease.scope: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sporadic, familial, variant), rapidly progressive dementia, startle myoclonus, ataxia, 14-3-3 protein, RT-QuIC, periodic sharp wave complexes, spongiform encephalopathy
prion-disease.core: Cognitive decline over weeks to months with stimulus-sensitive jerks and cerebellar dysfunction suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sporadic CJD usually older adults; familial cases involve autosomal dominant PRNP variants
Iatrogenic: contaminated neurosurgical equipment/tissue; variant CJD: bovine spongiform encephalopathy-contaminated beef

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Rapid progression** to akinetic mutism; visual, pyramidal, or extrapyramidal abnormalities
Startle myoclonus often develops after initial behavioral or memory changes
Variant CJD: younger age, early psychiatric symptoms and painful sensory complaints; prolonged course

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Misfolded protein templates conversion of normal prion protein; no nucleic acid
Neuronal loss, gliosis and vacuolation → spongiform encephalopathy without prominent inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Brain **MRI DWI**: cortical ribboning and caudate/putamen diffusion restriction
★ CSF **RT-QuIC** detects abnormal prion seeding; high specificity
CSF 14-3-3 reflects rapid neuronal injury; supportive but nonspecific
EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes; absence does not exclude disease
Exclude treatable mimics: CSF inflammatory/infectious studies, metabolic testing, autoimmune evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Supportive/palliative care**; no established disease-modifying treatment
Clonazepam or levetiracetam for distressing myoclonus; nutrition and caregiver support
Brain biopsy rarely needed; notify infection control before invasive tissue procedures

rows.label: Complications
items: Dysphagia, aspiration, immobility; sporadic CJD usually fatal within one year

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prion-specific instrument decontamination or disposal; routine sterilization insufficient
Familial disease → genetic counseling; casual contact does not transmit CJD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autoimmune encephalitis: seizures, inflammatory findings; potentially immunotherapy-responsive
Alzheimer disease: progression over years
Wernicke encephalopathy: malnutrition, ophthalmoplegia; treat promptly with IV thiamine

prion-disease.evidence: Diagnosis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC CJD overview](https://www.cdc.gov/creutzfeldt-jakob/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); established supportive care.

spinal-cord-compression.name: Spinal cord compression
spinal-cord-compression.scope: Neoplastic spinal cord compression (epidural metastases, dexamethasone, emergent MRI), spinal epidural abscess (fever, IV drug use, empiric antibiotics), cauda equina syndrome, surgical decompression
spinal-cord-compression.core: Back pain with new weakness, sensory changes or sphincter dysfunction requires urgent MRI to identify reversible neural compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known breast, prostate, lung, renal cancer or myeloma → epidural metastases
IV drug use, bacteremia, diabetes, spinal procedure or immunosuppression → epidural abscess
Large lumbar disc herniation, trauma or spinal stenosis → cauda equina compression
Anticoagulation + epidural catheter placement/removal → **spinal epidural hematoma**: acute paraplegia, incontinence

rows.label: Clues
items: Progressive nocturnal pain, pain with cough/strain, radicular symptoms; deficits may be initially subtle
Cord lesion: sensory level, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia below lesion after acute phase
★ Cauda equina: **saddle anesthesia, urinary retention**, reduced anal tone, asymmetric flaccid leg weakness
Epidural abscess: fever/back pain ± deficit; classic triad often incomplete

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epidural tumor, infection or disc material compresses neural tissue and impairs blood supply
Longstanding compression produces irreversible ischemic injury; bladder dysfunction signals advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urgent contrast MRI** of suspected region; whole spine for suspected metastatic compression
Postvoid residual supports retention assessment but normal result does not exclude early cauda equina syndrome
Suspected abscess → blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP; image before LP
MRI unavailable/contraindicated → CT myelography; ordinary radiographs cannot exclude epidural pathology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Malignant compression with deficit → **dexamethasone immediately**, urgent neurosurgery/radiation consultation
Tumor → decompression/stabilization ± radiotherapy; choice depends on stability, neurologic function and prognosis
★ Epidural abscess → **vancomycin + cefepime**, cultures; urgent decompression for deficits or instability
Cauda equina syndrome → emergency spinal surgical assessment and **decompression**
Immobilize if instability suspected; bladder drainage and analgesia during definitive treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent paralysis, bowel/bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, pressure injuries and VTE
Abscess → sepsis; steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rapid assessment of cancer-associated new back pain; sterile procedures and prompt bacteremia treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mechanical strain: normal neurologic exam, no sphincter symptoms
Transverse myelitis: intrinsic cord lesion without external compression
Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetric findings without sensory level

spinal-cord-compression.evidence: Not checked online; established neurologic and oncologic emergency principles.

spinal-cord-injury.name: Spinal cord injury
spinal-cord-injury.scope: Traumatic spinal cord injury, incomplete cord syndromes, neurogenic shock, dermatome mapping, vertebral level
spinal-cord-injury.core: Trauma with weakness, a sensory level, and sphincter dysfunction demands spinal protection and urgent imaging; neurologic level may differ from vertebral injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Motor vehicle collision, falls, diving, penetrating injury; cervical stenosis predisposes to hyperextension injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute spinal shock: flaccid areflexia below lesion; later spasticity/hyperreflexia; assess sacral sparing
★ **Neurogenic shock**: hypotension, bradycardia, warm skin after high cord injury; exclude hemorrhage first
C3–5 involvement threatens diaphragmatic function; priapism and urinary retention support cord disruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Primary cord damage + secondary edema/ischemia; sympathetic interruption causes vasodilation and unopposed vagal tone

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ABCs with **cervical immobilization** → CT spine for fracture; persistent neurologic deficits → **MRI**
Document motor/sensory level, rectal tone, perianal sensation; S4–5 sparing defines incomplete injury
Dermatomes: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, S4–5 perianal
Motor: C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction
Upper thoracic segments ≈2 levels above same-numbered vertebrae; cord ends L1–2; lower injuries → nerve roots

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Support ventilation, avoid hypoxia/hypotension; hemorrhage → blood; neurogenic shock → cautious fluids, **norepinephrine**
Urgent decompression/stabilization for compressive or unstable injuries; early specialist transfer
★ **No routine high-dose methylprednisolone**; harms exceed benefit; older exam questions may expect it after blunt injury
Rehabilitation, pressure relief, intermittent catheterization, bowel regimen, VTE prophylaxis
Autonomic dysreflexia → sit upright, loosen clothing, empty bladder; persistent severe hypertension → topical nitroglycerin

rows.label: Complications
items: Autonomic dysreflexia after injury ≥T6: bladder/bowel trigger → severe hypertension, headache, sweating above lesion
Pressure injuries, DVT/PE, recurrent UTI, respiratory failure, contractures, chronic neuropathic pain

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seatbelts, helmets, fall prevention, safe diving; maintain skin checks and bladder/bowel schedules

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cauda equina: asymmetric radicular pain, saddle anesthesia, LMN weakness, reduced reflexes
Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexia without discrete sensory level; often preceding infection

table.title: Incomplete cord syndromes
rows: Ipsilateral motor/vibration; contralateral pain/temperature starts 1–2 levels below

spinal-cord-injury.evidence: Autonomic dysreflexia checked 2026-10-30: [PVA clinician guideline](https://pva.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/cpg_autonomic-dysreflexia.pdf); remaining acute management: established trauma teaching.

spondyloarthritis.name: Spondyloarthritis
spondyloarthritis.scope: Ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, enteropathic arthritis, HLA-B27, sacroiliitis
spondyloarthritis.core: Seronegative inflammatory arthritis characterized by axial pain, enthesitis, or asymmetric peripheral arthritis; identify associated skin, eye, bowel, and genitourinary disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Onset usually before age 45; family history and **HLA-B27** association, strongest in axial disease
Immune-mediated predisposition; preceding Chlamydia or enteric infection can trigger reactive arthritis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Morning stiffness >30 minutes**, nocturnal back pain, improvement with exercise rather than rest
Alternating buttock pain, reduced spinal mobility/chest expansion; Achilles/plantar enthesitis, dactylitis
★ Painful photophobic red eye → **anterior uveitis**, urgent ophthalmology

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation at entheses and sacroiliac joints → erosions followed by new bone formation/ankylosis
TNF and IL-17 pathways drive disease; RF/anti-CCP usually absent

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pelvic radiograph** for sacroiliitis; persistent suspicion with normal radiograph → **MRI sacroiliac joints**
ESR/CRP support activity but may be normal; HLA-B27 neither confirms nor excludes disease
Effusion → aspirate if infection/crystals possible; reactive arthritis → exposure-directed Chlamydia NAAT

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Exercise/physical therapy + NSAID**, e.g., naproxen; avoid prolonged immobilization
Persistent active axial disease → TNF inhibitor, e.g., adalimumab, or IL-17 inhibitor, e.g., secukinumab
Peripheral arthritis → methotrexate/sulfasalazine, ineffective for purely axial disease; avoid chronic systemic steroids
Active IBD/recurrent uveitis → monoclonal TNF inhibitor preferred; avoid IL-17 blockade in active IBD
Treat active Chlamydia and partners; antibiotics do not routinely resolve established postinfectious arthritis

rows.label: Complications
items: Spinal fusion, osteoporosis and unstable vertebral fracture after minor trauma
Aortic regurgitation/conduction disease in longstanding axial disease; biologics → serious infection/TB reactivation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, posture and extension exercises; fall precautions when spine ankylosed
Before biologics: TB/HBV testing and vaccination; sexual barrier protection reduces Chlamydia-associated episodes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mechanical back pain: worse with activity, improved with rest, minimal morning stiffness
Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetric small-joint synovitis, usually no sacroiliitis; anti-CCP often positive
DISH: older adults, flowing anterior ligament ossification, preserved sacroiliac joints

table.title: Phenotypes
rows: Psoriasis, nail pitting, DIP arthritis; pencil-in-cup
Postinfection oligoarthritis; urethritis, conjunctivitis may coexist
Crohn/UC; peripheral arthritis often tracks bowel activity

status-epilepticus.name: Status epilepticus
status-epilepticus.scope: Generalized convulsive status epilepticus, first-line benzodiazepines, second-line antiepileptics, refractory status, reversible causes
status-epilepticus.core: Generalized convulsive seizure lasting ≥5 minutes, or recurrent seizures without recovery between them: treat immediately while seeking reversible causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antiseizure medication, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, acute stroke, hemorrhage, tumor, CNS infection
Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia; stimulant or isoniazid toxicity; eclampsia

rows.label: Clues
items: Bilateral tonic-clonic activity, impaired consciousness, cyanosis, autonomic activation
★ Convulsions stop but consciousness fails to improve → suspect **nonconvulsive status**, not simply sedation
Subtle eye deviation, eyelid/facial twitching may be the only visible ongoing seizure activity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sustained excitation and diminishing inhibitory responsiveness → neuronal injury, hypermetabolism, treatment resistance
Hypoxia and systemic metabolic derangements amplify brain injury as seizure duration increases

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside glucose immediately**; electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal/liver tests, drug levels, toxicology when relevant
Head CT after stabilization for new focal signs, trauma, or unexplained first episode
★ Persistent impaired awareness/refractory seizure → **continuous EEG**; imaging never delays anticonvulsants
Fever/meningismus → blood cultures, empiric antimicrobials; LP after stabilization and mass-effect assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, oxygen, suction, IV/IO access; hypoglycemia → dextrose; malnutrition → thiamine without delaying glucose
★ **IV lorazepam** first; no IV access → **IM midazolam**; repeat benzodiazepine once if needed
★ Persistent seizure → IV loading **levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate**; similar second-line efficacy
Benzodiazepine + second-line failure → intubation, ICU, propofol or midazolam infusion guided by continuous EEG
Eclampsia → magnesium; severe hyponatremia → hypertonic saline; isoniazid → pyridoxine; withdrawal → benzodiazepines

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, hypoxic brain injury, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis, hyperthermia; arrhythmias and death
Sedatives → respiratory depression/hypotension; fosphenytoin → arrhythmia; valproate → hepatotoxicity/hyperammonemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, rescue seizure plan, treatment of precipitating disease; supervised sedative/alcohol withdrawal
Maintain antiseizure therapy before anesthetic withdrawal; driving restrictions, seizure precautions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG lacks ictal correlate; do not diagnose from one bedside sign
Convulsive syncope: brief jerks with rapid recovery; cardiovascular trigger
Postictal state: gradually improving awareness; EEG excludes ongoing electrical seizures when uncertain

status-epilepticus.evidence: Treatment checked 2026-10-30: [ACEP clinical policy, 2024](https://www.acepnow.com/article/acep-clinical-policy-on-seizures/); [AES convulsive status guideline, 2016](https://www.acep.org/siteassets/uploads/uploaded-files/acep/clinical-and-practice-management/clinical-policies/aesconvulsivestatusepilepticus.pdf).

superior-vena-cava-syndrome.name: Superior vena cava syndrome
superior-vena-cava-syndrome.scope: Small cell lung cancer, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, indwelling intravascular catheters, facial edema, venous distention, Pemberton sign, CT chest with IV contrast, radiation therapy, endovascular stenting
superior-vena-cava-syndrome.core: Facial and upper-extremity swelling with distended chest/neck veins suggests obstruction of central venous drainage above the right atrium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Lung malignancy, especially central tumors; non-Hodgkin lymphoma; mediastinal mass
Central venous catheters, pacemaker leads → thrombosis/stenosis; prior mediastinal radiation

rows.label: Clues
items: Symptoms worsen supine or bending forward; head fullness, dyspnea, cough, upper-body cyanosis
**Pemberton sign**: arm elevation produces facial congestion/distress; suggests thoracic inlet obstruction
★ **Stridor, altered mental status, syncope or severe hypoxemia** → life-threatening obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extrinsic compression or intraluminal thrombus raises upper-body venous pressure; collateral veins develop
Rapid obstruction produces more severe symptoms than slowly progressive occlusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable patient → **CT chest with IV contrast** to define lesion, thrombus and collateral pathways
Obtain tissue diagnosis from accessible node or bronchoscopic/image-guided biopsy before tumor-directed treatment when stable
Duplex ultrasound evaluates associated upper-extremity thrombosis but cannot reliably exclude intrathoracic obstruction

rows.label: Tx
items: Elevate head, oxygen, assess airway; urgent interventional radiology/oncology input
★ Severe airway/cerebral compromise → **endovascular stenting** for rapid relief; do not await histology
★ Stable malignancy → biopsy-guided chemotherapy, radiation or both; lymphoma/small-cell tumors often chemotherapy-responsive
Catheter-associated thrombus → anticoagulation, usually ≥3 months; remove catheter if unnecessary, infected or malfunctioning
Extensive acute thrombus → consider catheter intervention; steroids for selected responsive tumors/airway edema

rows.label: Complications
items: Laryngeal edema, cerebral edema, venous thrombosis; stent thrombosis or migration
Empiric radiation/steroids before biopsy may obscure lymphoma diagnosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Minimize unnecessary central catheter duration; smoking cessation; reassess vascular devices with recurrent thrombosis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Heart failure: lower-extremity edema and broader volume-overload pattern
Angioedema: abrupt lip/tongue swelling without collateral chest veins
Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, JVD, pericardial effusion; no upper-body venous obstruction on CT

superior-vena-cava-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established stabilization, tissue-diagnosis and cause-directed management.

sympathomimetic-toxicity.name: Sympathomimetic toxicity
sympathomimetic-toxicity.scope: Cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine, sympathomimetic toxidrome, benzodiazepines, cooling, avoidance of pure beta-blockers
sympathomimetic-toxicity.core: Stimulant exposure produces agitation, diaphoresis, mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia; sedation limits dangerous catecholamine excess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine, synthetic cathinones; prescription stimulant misuse
Coingested alcohol forms cocaethylene with cocaine, increasing cardiotoxicity; exertion/heat worsens injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Paranoia, psychosis, seizures, chest pain; bowel sounds usually active
★ **Severe hyperthermia, acidosis, rigidity/agitation, arrhythmia** → life-threatening poisoning
Cocaine additionally blocks sodium channels, producing QRS widening
MDMA: bruxism, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, severe **hyponatremia** from water intake and SIADH

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cocaine inhibits monoamine reuptake; amphetamines increase release → adrenergic/dopaminergic overstimulation
Vasoconstriction, increased oxygen demand, platelet activation → myocardial/cerebral ischemia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical toxidrome**; temperature, glucose, ECG, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis
Chest pain → serial ECG/troponin; neurologic deficit/severe headache → head CT for hemorrhage/stroke
Urine immunoassay supports exposure but false positives/negatives occur; never delay stabilization for results

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Benzodiazepines first** for agitation, seizures, tachycardia, hypertension; airway support when necessary
★ **Rapid external cooling + IV crystalloids** for hyperthermia/rhabdomyolysis; antipyretics ineffective
Persistent severe hypertension/vasospasm → nitroglycerin, nicardipine, or phentolamine after sedation
★ Acute cocaine toxicity: **avoid pure beta-blocker monotherapy**; unopposed alpha vasoconstriction concern
Wide QRS ventricular toxicity → sodium bicarbonate; ACS evaluation and aspirin when bleeding contraindications absent

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, aortic dissection, ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC
Methamphetamine: formication, dental decay, psychosis, cardiomyopathy; cocaine snorting: rhinitis, septal perforation; pregnancy: abruption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Offer addiction treatment and contingency management; assess depression and suicidality after stimulant crash
Harm-reduction counseling, avoid mixing substances; naloxone access for possible opioid contamination

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anticholinergic toxicity: dry skin, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds
Serotonin syndrome: inducible/spontaneous clonus, hyperreflexia; NMS: dopamine blockade, lead-pipe rigidity
Thyroid storm: thyroid disease with sustained systemic hypermetabolism
PCP: rotatory/vertical nystagmus, violent agitation; also sedate with benzodiazepines

syncope.name: Syncope
syncope.scope: Vasovagal / neurocardiogenic syncope, orthostatic syncope, situational syncope, cardiogenic syncope, breath-holding spells, cerebral hypoperfusion workup
syncope.core: Brief loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid spontaneous recovery; identify cardiac danger before labeling an episode reflex-mediated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dehydration, blood loss, autonomic dysfunction, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-1 blockers; prolonged standing, heat, fear
Structural heart disease, conduction disease, arrhythmias, family history of sudden death

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Exertional or supine syncope**, palpitations, absent prodrome, cardiac murmur → high-risk cause
Reflex prodrome: nausea, warmth, diaphoresis, tunnel vision; may include brief myoclonic jerks
Situational triggers: urination, coughing, defecation; breath-holding spells follow crying/pain in young children
Shaving, tight collar, head turning + bradycardia → **carotid sinus hypersensitivity**; confirm with carotid sinus massage

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Vasodilation/bradycardia, failed postural compensation, or low cardiac output transiently limits cerebral flow

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Initial **history, examination, orthostatic BP, ECG**; bedside glucose and targeted pregnancy/bleeding evaluation
Orthostasis: systolic fall ≥20 or diastolic ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes standing
High-risk → admission/monitoring; suspected structural disease → echo; intermittent arrhythmia → ambulatory ECG
Tilt-table testing for recurrent unexplained reflex/orthostatic cases; no routine head CT, EEG, carotid ultrasound
Typical breath-holding spells: normal development, awake trigger, rapid recovery; CBC/ferritin and ECG when evaluating

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reflex event → supine, legs elevated; **hydration, counterpressure maneuvers**, trigger recognition
Orthostatic cause → replace volume, review drugs, rise slowly, compression; refractory neurogenic cases → midodrine
★ Cardiac cause → **treat rhythm/obstruction**, restrict unsafe activity pending evaluation
Breath-holding: reassure caregivers, safe positioning, treat iron deficiency; no antiseizure drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, fractures, driving injury; underlying cardiac disease carries sudden-death risk
Recurrent episodes → activity limitation, anxiety; pressor drugs can cause supine hypertension

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid dehydration and prolonged immobility; individualized driving/activity restrictions after unexplained or cardiac events

rows.label: Mimics
items: Seizure: prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue biting; incontinence occurs in both
Hypoglycemia: persistent altered state until glucose corrected
TIA: focal deficit; isolated transient unconsciousness unusual

syncope.evidence: Not checked online; established syncope evaluation teaching.

syringomyelia.name: Syringomyelia
syringomyelia.scope: Cervical spinal cord syrinx, Chiari I malformation association, post-traumatic syrinx, cape-like dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature), anterior white commissure, MRI cervical spine
syringomyelia.core: A spinal cord syrinx classically causes bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration and position sense.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Chiari I malformation**, prior spinal cord trauma; also intramedullary tumor, arachnoid scarring, tethering
Post-traumatic syrinx may emerge years after injury; no recent trauma necessary

rows.label: Clues
items: Unrecognized burns or hand injuries; neuropathic neck/shoulder pain; sensory distribution may be asymmetric
★ Segmental **hand weakness, wasting, reduced reflexes** as anterior horns become involved
Larger syrinx → leg spasticity/hyperreflexia from corticospinal involvement; late bladder/bowel dysfunction
Hindbrain involvement: occipital Valsalva headache, ataxia, nystagmus; progressive bulbar symptoms → prompt assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CSF-filled intramedullary cavity expands through central gray matter
★ Crossing spinothalamic fibers injured in **anterior white commissure**; dorsal columns initially spared
Disordered CSF flow, especially at craniocervical junction, promotes cavity formation and enlargement

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI cervical spine** confirms cavity; extend imaging to brain/craniocervical junction and remaining cord
Contrast MRI if tumor suspected; CSF-flow imaging helps selected surgical planning
Document motor, reflex, sensory, gait and sphincter baseline; repeat imaging if symptoms progress
Plain radiographs cannot exclude intramedullary disease; lumbar puncture does not establish diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: Asymptomatic stable cavity → neurosurgical/neurologic observation with examinations and interval MRI
★ Progressive deficits or symptomatic Chiari-associated syrinx → **posterior fossa decompression** restoring CSF flow
Tumor-related disease → tumor-directed surgery; selected persistent syrinx → drainage/shunting
Gabapentin for neuropathic pain; rehabilitation and occupational adaptations; surgery may not reverse established deficits

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent hand atrophy, spastic paresis, chronic pain, scoliosis, neuropathic arthropathy
Syringobulbia → dysphagia/respiratory dysfunction; shunt obstruction or recurrence after surgery

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protect insensate skin from burns/cuts; inspect hands and regulate bath-water temperature
Avoid heavy straining that provokes symptoms; report new weakness, gait change, or sphincter dysfunction promptly

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy: neck degeneration, cord compression, often dorsal-column or root findings
ALS: combined motor neuron signs without sensory loss
Brown-Séquard syndrome: ipsilateral weakness/proprioception loss with contralateral pain/temperature deficit

toxic-alcohol-poisoning.name: Toxic alcohol poisoning
toxic-alcohol-poisoning.scope: Ethylene glycol (calcium oxalate, renal failure), methanol (visual impairment, optic disc hyperemia), isopropyl alcohol (ketosis without acidosis), osmolar gap, fomepizole, hemodialysis
toxic-alcohol-poisoning.core: Unexplained intoxication with an osmolar gap suggests toxic alcohol exposure; delayed organic-acid accumulation can produce profound anion-gap acidosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Antifreeze, windshield-washer fluid, solvents; accidental ingestion or self-harm; substitute alcohol consumption

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting, abdominal pain, altered consciousness; tachypnea or shock signals severe toxicity
★ **Normal osmolar gap does not exclude late poisoning**; history may be unavailable

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts parent alcohols into characteristic metabolites
Parent compounds elevate osmolar gap early; metabolites later raise anion gap in acid-producing ingestions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Electrolytes, ABG/VBG, glucose, BUN, measured osmolality, ethanol and specific alcohol levels
Calculated osmolality = 2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; add ethanol/4.6, concentrations in mg/dL
Measured minus calculated >10 mOsm/kg supports exposure; nonspecific and time-dependent
Urinalysis and calcium/creatinine assess organ injury; absent characteristic sediment inclusions do not exclude exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway, IV fluids, poison-center consultation; **fomepizole** immediately for suspected methanol/ethylene glycol
Methanol: vision loss, coma/seizures or pH ≤7.15 → **hemodialysis**; ethylene glycol: severe acidosis/AKI → dialysis
Sodium bicarbonate for marked acidemia; methanol → folinic acid; ethylene glycol → thiamine/pyridoxine adjuncts
★ Isopropanol → supportive care; **avoid fomepizole**, which prolongs parent-compound toxicity

rows.label: Complications
items: Methanol: permanent blindness, basal ganglia injury
Oxalate toxicity: hypocalcemic dysrhythmias; any ingestion: aspiration, coma, death

rows.label: Prevention
items: Store products separately from beverages; child-resistant containers; suicide-risk assessment after intentional ingestion

rows.label: Mimics
items: DKA: hyperglycemia and β-hydroxybutyrate elevation
Alcoholic ketoacidosis: poor intake after alcohol binge, low/normal glucose

toxic-alcohol-poisoning.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [EXTRIP methanol](https://www.extrip-workgroup.org/methanol), [ethylene glycol](https://www.extrip-workgroup.org/ethylene-glycol); other principles: established toxicology teaching.

traumatic-brain-injury.name: Traumatic brain injury
traumatic-brain-injury.scope: Epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, cerebral contusion, diffuse axonal injury, concussion, elevated ICP
traumatic-brain-injury.core: Head trauma ranges from transient functional disturbance to expanding hemorrhage; serial neurologic deterioration requires urgent imaging and neurosurgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Falls, crashes, assault, sports; anticoagulants, antiplatelets, bleeding disorders
Older age, alcohol use and cerebral atrophy predispose to bridging-vein injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Headache, vomiting, amnesia; focal deficit or progressive somnolence suggests structural injury; hemiparesis → contralateral supratentorial mass
★ **Unilateral fixed dilated pupil + declining consciousness** → uncal herniation
Cushing response: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing; late sign of ↑ICP

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impact/shear → ischemia, excitotoxicity; **cerebral edema** → deterioration over 1–3 days, brainstem reflex loss
Rising intracranial volume → ↓cerebral perfusion; hypotension/hypoxia worsen secondary injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ABCs/cervical protection → **GCS, pupils, focal examination**, repeated serially
**Noncontrast head CT** for moderate/severe injury or mild injury with high-risk features
High-risk features: anticoagulation, skull-fracture signs, focal deficit, repeated vomiting, worsening symptoms
GCS 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, ≤8 severe

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **GCS ≤8 or hypoventilation → intubate before imaging/surgery**; avoid hypoxemia/hypotension; reverse anticoagulants
Expanding hematoma, mass effect or deterioration → urgent neurosurgical evacuation
★ Elevated ICP → head elevation, analgesia/sedation, **hypertonic saline or mannitol**; treat sustained ICP >22 mm Hg
Herniation → brief hyperventilation as bridge; no prophylactic hyperventilation or corticosteroids
Severe/high-risk TBI → levetiracetam for 7 days; refractory ICP → neurosurgical decompression

rows.label: Complications
items: Posttraumatic seizures, chronic cognitive/behavioral impairment, postconcussion syndrome, hydrocephalus
Skull-base fracture → CSF leak/meningitis; no nasal instrumentation
Frontal contusion → **executive dysfunction**: impaired conceptual planning, judgment, motivation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seatbelts, helmets, fall prevention
Concussion: no same-day sports; relative rest 24–48 hours → graded recovery
Persistent symptoms, even normal CT → **no contact sports** until reassessed; second-impact risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Intoxication: may coexist; exclude intracranial injury first
Hypoglycemia: check glucose in any altered mental status

table.title: Injury patterns
rows: Temporal impact; middle meningeal artery; lucid interval
Bridging-vein rupture; acute or weeks-later fluctuating decline
Crescent; crosses sutures, limited by dural reflections
Immediate prolonged coma after rotational acceleration
Transient LOC, amnesia, headache, vomiting; normal neurologic exam

traumatic-brain-injury.evidence: Acute management checked 2026-10-30: [ACS TBI best practices, 2024](https://www.facs.org/media/vgfgjpfk/best-practices-guidelines-traumatic-brain-injury.pdf).

tuberculosis.name: Tuberculosis
tuberculosis.scope: Latent TB infection screening (PPD, IGRA), treatment regimens, active pulmonary TB, acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, RIPE therapy, extrapulmonary TB (Pott disease)
tuberculosis.core: Chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and upper-lobe cavitation suggest contagious pulmonary tuberculosis; latent infection has no active disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Close contact, endemic residence, incarceration, homelessness, crowding, **long-term care** work/volunteering
HIV, TNF inhibitors, transplant, silicosis, diabetes → progression/reactivation risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Hemoptysis, prolonged fever; primary disease may cause hilar adenopathy or pleural effusion
★ **Back pain with vertebral destruction** → Pott disease; miliary spread causes diffuse micronodules
Tuberculous pleurisy: **lymphocytic exudate**, high protein, low glucose

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Airborne bacilli survive in macrophages; T-cell granulomas contain infection; T-cell dysfunction → reactivation, skin-test anergy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Screening: **IGRA** preferred after BCG; TST read induration at 48–72 hours
Positive screening → symptoms + chest radiograph; neither test distinguishes latent from active infection
★ Active suspicion → **sputum NAAT, AFB smear, culture and susceptibility**; collect serial specimens
Negative smear, TST or IGRA does not exclude active TB, especially with immunosuppression or malnutrition
Pott suspicion → spinal MRI, biopsy/culture; assess cord compression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected contagious disease → **airborne isolation** and public-health notification
Drug-susceptible active TB: 2 months isoniazid/rifampin/pyrazinamide/ethambutol → 4 months isoniazid/rifampin
Eligible pulmonary cases ≥12 years: 4-month isoniazid/rifapentine/moxifloxacin/pyrazinamide-based regimen alternative
Latent, no RIPE: 3-month isoniazid/rifapentine or 4-month rifampin; older questions may expect **isoniazid** alone, still acceptable
Isoniazid → pyridoxine prevents neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia; Pott with deficit/instability → urgent spinal surgery evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Meningitis, adrenal destruction, spinal cord compression, bronchiectasis
INH/rifampin/pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity; ethambutol: optic neuropathy; rifampin: enzyme induction, orange secretions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Contact investigation**, latent-treatment completion; directly observed active treatment improves adherence
Review drug interactions and baseline liver risk; monitor visual acuity/color vision with ethambutol

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung cancer: focal malignant biopsy
Fungal infection: geographic exposure; nontuberculous mycobacteria: species identification distinguishes

table.title: Positive TST thresholds
rows: HIV, close contacts, transplant, substantial immunosuppression
Healthcare workers, exposure-risk groups, comorbidities, young children

vertigo.name: Vertigo
vertigo.scope: Peripheral vs central vertigo, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (Dix-Hallpike, Epley maneuver), vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis, Meniere disease, vestibular migraine
vertigo.core: Illusion of movement: timing, triggers, hearing findings and neurologic examination distinguish benign vestibular disease from posterior-circulation ischemia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, vascular risk factors → central ischemia; recent viral illness, head injury or migraine history
Ototoxic drugs and ear disease can cause peripheral vestibular injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Peripheral: horizontal-torsional unidirectional nystagmus, reduced with fixation; no focal neurologic deficit
★ **Vertical/direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation, severe truncal ataxia or focal deficits** → central concern
New unilateral hearing loss with continuous acute vertigo can represent AICA stroke, not simply labyrinthitis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Asymmetric vestibular input → movement illusion and nystagmus; central lesions involve brainstem/cerebellum
BPPV: displaced **otoliths (canaliths)** in semicircular canal → position-triggered endolymph movement

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Dix-Hallpike** for triggered episodic symptoms; typical upbeat torsional nystagmus has latency and fatigues
Continuous acute syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus → **HINTS by trained clinician**; not for brief positional episodes
★ Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew → **stroke evaluation/MRI ± CTA/MRA**
Untrained examiner or concerning findings → MRI; early diffusion imaging may miss posterior stroke
Typical BPPV → no routine imaging; suspected Meniere → audiometry; horizontal positional nystagmus → supine-roll test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Central concern → urgent **stroke pathway**; negative head CT cannot exclude posterior infarction
Severe acute nausea → brief meclizine/ondansetron; prolonged vestibular suppressants impair compensation

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, dehydration, impaired driving; missed stroke → disability/death; recurrent inner-ear disease → hearing loss

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall precautions, avoid driving during attacks; reduce individual migraine triggers and address vascular risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Orthostatic hypotension: standing-triggered presyncope with BP drop, rather than head-position-triggered nystagmus
Arrhythmia: episodic faintness/palpitations; ECG or monitoring establishes cardiac cause

table.title: Peripheral and episodic patterns
rows: Rehabilitation; discuss early steroids, benefit uncertain
